    This vignette is the reference for Figure 1 of the paper. It sets out the simulation in enough detail to be reproduced, defines the three PIT-Wasserstein metrics briefly, and reads the four panels. The paper states the same material compactly in its methods section and refers back here for the full specification.

    If you are new to calibration or to the probability integral transform, read vignette("introduction-to-pit") first. For the null distributions and pp-values, see vignette("significance-testing").

    1. The simulation

    The difficulty in evaluating a calibration metric is that real forecasters do not come with their miscalibration written on the label. So we simulate estimators whose failure mode we fix by construction, and ask what each metric reports.

    1.1 The error-function model

    Each simulated estimator is defined by two distributions, following the structure introduced in vignette("introduction-to-pit"):

    Component Symbol Role
    error distribution ℰ∼𝒩(μℰ,σℰ)\mathcal{E} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_\mathcal{E}, \sigma_\mathcal{E}) how far the estimator’s central estimate lands from the truth
    spread distribution 𝒮∼LogNormal(σ𝒮,κ𝒮)\mathcal{S} \sim \mathrm{LogNormal}(\sigma_\mathcal{S}, \kappa_\mathcal{S}) what uncertainty the estimator claims

    For each of the estimator’s predictions ii we draw a true value xix_i, an error ei∼ℰe_i \sim \mathcal{E} and a claimed uncertainty si∼𝒮s_i \sim \mathcal{S}, and emit the probabilistic prediction

    X̂i∼𝒩(xi+ei,si) \hat{X}_i \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(x_i + e_i,\; s_i\right)

    Three parameters therefore control everything, and they are independent:

    • μℰ\mu_\mathcal{E} — bias. The systematic displacement of the central estimate. Zero means unbiased.
    • σ𝒮/σℰ\sigma_\mathcal{S}/\sigma_\mathcal{E} — dispersion calibration, written calibration in the code and plotted on every x-axis below. This is the ratio of the uncertainty the estimator claims to the uncertainty it actually has. One is perfect; below one is over-confident; above one is conservative.
    • κ𝒮\kappa_\mathcal{S} — spread–error decoupling, labelled “CI variation” in the figures. The coefficient of variation of the claimed uncertainty. Zero means every prediction claims the same width. Larger values mean the stated uncertainty varies from prediction to prediction without tracking the realised error, which is miscalibration even when the average width is right.

    The spread distribution is lognormal (lnorm4, parametrised by median and coefficient of variation) because a claimed uncertainty must be positive and because it makes κ𝒮\kappa_\mathcal{S} scale-free.

    1.2 The parameter sweep

    We simulate 1000 estimators, each making 1000 predictions, with the three parameters drawn independently so that the whole space is covered rather than a grid of special cases:

    Parameter Drawn as Range
    true values xix_i Uniform(−1,1)\mathrm{Uniform}(-1, 1) per prediction
    bias μℰ\mu_\mathcal{E} Uniform(−1,1)\mathrm{Uniform}(-1, 1) per estimator
    error scale σℰ\sigma_\mathcal{E} log\log-uniform [12,2][\tfrac12, 2]
    claimed scale σ𝒮\sigma_\mathcal{S} log\log-uniform [12,2][\tfrac12, 2]
    decoupling κ𝒮\kappa_\mathcal{S} Uniform(0,2)\mathrm{Uniform}(0, 2) per estimator

    Drawing σ𝒮\sigma_\mathcal{S} and σℰ\sigma_\mathcal{E} independently and log-uniformly gives a dispersion calibration ratio spanning [14,4][\tfrac14, 4], symmetric on the log scale — which matters, because an estimator twice too wide and one twice too narrow are equally wrong and the metric should say so.

    Crucially, bias is drawn independently of dispersion calibration. Each point in the figures is an estimator with its own arbitrary combination of the three, so if a metric conflates bias with dispersion error it will show up as vertical scatter coloured by bias.

    bias_limit = 1
conf_range = 2

config = tibble(
  sd_sd_mean = c(conf_range),
  sd_label = forcats::as_factor(c("heterogenous CIs"))
) %>%
  group_by(sd_label, sd_sd_mean) %>%
  reframe(
    samples = 1000,
    bias_dist = "norm",
    bias_location = runif(1000, -bias_limit, bias_limit),
    bias_scale = exp(runif(1000, -log(conf_range), log(conf_range))),
    sharpness_dist = "lnorm4",
    sharpness_location = exp(runif(1000, -log(conf_range), log(conf_range))),
    sharpness_scale = runif(1000, 0, sd_sd_mean)
  )

    generate_simulation() expands that configuration into 1000 × 1000 individual predictions, and prediction_scores() collapses each estimator’s 1000 predictions back to one row of scores.

    sim = config %>% generate_simulation(true_value_fn = function(n) runif(n, -1, 1))
#> interfacer: development mode active (test environment).
#> This message is displayed once every 8 hours.
#> Warning: unexpected groups in the return value of generate_simulation(...):
#> observed: sd_label+sd_sd_mean+samples+bias_dist+bias_location+bias_scale+sharpness_dist+sharpness_location+sharpness_scale+link+dist+run_id+calibration+adjust
#> expected: <any>+dist+link+calibration+adjust
#> Warning: ireturn validation did not pass without changing the value.
scores = sim %>% prediction_scores()

    2. The metrics

    Full definitions and derivations are in the paper; this is the working summary. For each estimator, the PIT values ui=Fi(xi)u_i = F_i(x_i) are sorted and compared against the uniform plotting positions ri=(i−12)/nr_i = (i - \tfrac12)/n:

    Bpit=1n∑i|ri−u(i)| B_{pit} = \frac1n\sum_i \left| r_i - u_{(i)} \right|

    which is the 1-Wasserstein distance between the empirical PIT distribution and Uniform(0,1)\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1) — the area between the PIT histogram’s cumulative curve and the diagonal. It is zero for a calibrated estimator and grows with any departure, including a pure bias.

    The bias adjustment estimates one location shift, δ̂=mediani(g(mi)−g(xi))\hat\delta = \mathrm{median}_i(g(m_i) - g(x_i)) on the link scale, applies it to the observations, and recomputes the PIT values as uadju^{adj}. Applying the same two summaries to the adjusted values gives

    Upit=1n∑i|ri−u(i)adj|,Dpit=1n∑i(ri−u(i)adj)sgn(12−ri) U_{pit} = \frac1n\sum_i \left| r_i - u^{adj}_{(i)} \right|, \qquad D_{pit} = \frac1n\sum_i \left( r_i - u^{adj}_{(i)} \right)\mathrm{sgn}\!\left(\tfrac12 - r_i\right)

    UpitU_{pit} is the same undirected distance with the location error removed. DpitD_{pit} replaces the absolute value with a weight that is +1+1 below the median and −1-1 above it, so that departures at the two ends cancel instead of accumulating — which is what makes it signed, and positive for an over-confident estimator.

    Metric Range Reads
    BpitB_{pit} [0,12][0, \tfrac12] total miscalibration, bias included
    UpitU_{pit} [0,12][0, \tfrac12] miscalibration with bias removed
    DpitD_{pit} [−14,14][-\tfrac14, \tfrac14] signed dispersion error: ++ over-confident, −- conservative

    All three are returned by prediction_scores() alongside the mean CRPS and coverage probabilities.

    3. Figure 1

    The four panels plot each of the 1000 estimators against its true dispersion calibration σ𝒮/σℰ\sigma_\mathcal{S}/\sigma_\mathcal{E} on a log x-axis, with the vertical line at 1 marking perfect calibration. A metric that measures dispersion calibration should form a tight, monotone curve about that line; scatter is the metric responding to something else.

    # estimator SD/error SD:
# ratio between the SD of an estimate and the SD of the error function
# a low value means that the estimate is more confident than it should be
# a high value says it is too conservative

# Panel A: mean CRPS

p2a = ggplot(
  scores,
  aes(x = calibration, y = mean_crps, colour = abs(bias))
) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_color_viridis_c(name = "Absolute bias",option = "magma") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    label = "conservative >",
    x = 1,
    y = Inf,
    hjust = -0.5,
    vjust = 1.5,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    label = "< overconfident",
    x = 1,
    y = Inf,
    hjust = 1.5,
    vjust = 1.5,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  ylab("Mean CRPS") +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1) +
  xlab("estimator SD/error SD")

## Combined 4 panel plot

plot_metrics = patchwork::wrap_plots(
  p2a,

  plot_metrics,
  file.path(fig_dir, "fig1-metric-compare"),
  size = std_size$two_third,
  formats = c("pdf", "eps")
)

    Panel B, Mean CRPS The CRPS is a proper score and the standard summary of probabilistic forecast quality. Points are coloured by absolute bias.

    It does respond to dispersion calibration — the lower envelope of the cloud has a minimum near 1 — but the response is swamped. For any given value on the x-axis the CRPS varies by a factor of several, ordered almost entirely by colour: the dark points (unbiased) sit low and the light points (badly biased) sit high. CRPS is dominated by accuracy, which is what a proper score is for. Two estimators with identical dispersion calibration score very differently if one is biased, and an unbiased over-confident estimator can outscore a well-dispersed biased one.

    This is the gap the rest of the figure addresses. CRPS answers “which forecaster is better?”; none of these panels is trying to answer that. They ask “how is this forecaster wrong?”, which a single proper score cannot be expected to decompose.

    Reading the three PIT-Wasserstein panels together:

    Panel B, BpitB_{pit} (coloured by absolute bias) has the same V shape but, like CRPS, is stratified by colour: bias inflates it. BpitB_{pit} is the honest omnibus statistic — it answers “is anything wrong?” and a location error genuinely is something wrong — but it cannot tell you what.

    Panel C, UpitU_{pit} (coloured by CI variation aka skill-spread decoupling) is the same statistic after the bias adjustment. The colour stratification is gone: the points collapse onto a tight V with its minimum at 1. This is the central claim of the paper made as a picture — the same estimators, the same arbitrary biases, and the metric now responds to dispersion calibration alone. What vertical spread remains is ordered by the colour scale, i.e. by κ𝒮\kappa_\mathcal{S}: spread–error decoupling lifts the floor of the V above zero, correctly, because an estimator whose stated uncertainty varies without tracking its error is not calibrated however good its average width.

    Panel D, DpitD_{pit} (coloured by CI variation) is the signed version, and it crosses zero — monotonically — at exactly the point of perfect calibration. Negative is conservative, positive is over-confident, so the sign names the failure rather than merely detecting it. Two further properties are visible: the root does not move with κ𝒮\kappa_\mathcal{S} (the colours are mixed where the curve crosses zero, unlike in panel C), and the curve is close to symmetric about the crossing on the log scale.

    Together C and D are complementary rather than redundant: DpitD_{pit} locates and signs a width error, UpitU_{pit} picks up shape departures that DpitD_{pit} cancels away. vignette("significance-testing") turns that pairing into a formal procedure.

    The one-line summary: colour stratification in panels A and B reflects bias , and in C and D reflects spread-skill decoupling. That is the bias invariance the adjustment buys, and it is what makes the adjusted metrics diagnostic rather than merely descriptive.

    3.5 An aside: coverage probability

    The obvious alternative diagnostic is to ask how often the truth falls inside a stated interval. For comparison:

    
ggplot(
  scores,
  aes(x = calibration, y = mean_coverage.0.5, colour=sharpness_scale)
) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    label = "conservative >",
    x = 1,
    y = 0.5,
    hjust = -0.5,
    vjust = 0.5,
    angle = 90,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    label = "< overconfident",
    x = 1,
    y = 0.5,
    hjust = 1.5,
    vjust = 0.5,
    angle = 90,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    label = "conservative >",
    x = 1,
    y = 0.5,
    hjust = -0.5,
    vjust = 0.5,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    label = "< overconfident",
    x = 1,
    y = 0.5,
    hjust = 1.5,
    vjust = 0.5,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  ylab("50% coverage probability") +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(name = "CI variation") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  xlab("estimator SD/error SD")

    Coverage is monotone in dispersion calibration and has the right sign, so it is a usable diagnostic. Two things limit it. It saturates — the curve flattens at both ends, so it discriminates poorly among badly miscalibrated or biased estimators — and it is a single binary summary at one nominal level, throwing away everything the rest of the predictive distribution says. The PIT-Wasserstein metrics use the whole distribution and do not saturate.
